script.opening: “Hi. It’s about my periods. They’ve always been bad, but the last few years I’m having to take days off every month and work aren’t happy. I had a scan last year and they said it was normal, so I don’t really know what else can be done.”

facts.text: “It starts a couple of days before I bleed, low down in my tummy and into my back. Days one and two of the period I have to lie down with a hot water bottle. It used to be one bad day, now it’s four or five.” Pain score 8–9/10 at worst.
“Periods are regular, every 28 days, about six days long. Heavyish on day two but not flooding.” No bleeding between periods or after sex.
If asked sensitively: “Deep down it hurts during sex — like something’s being hit. It’s been like that about two years. We’ve kind of stopped.”
“When I’m on my period it really hurts to open my bowels.” No blood from the back passage, no blood in the urine, no change in bowel habit outside periods. No bloating between periods.
Some pain mid-cycle occasionally. No pain unrelated to periods most days.

“Mefenamic acid takes the edge off. I take it when the pain starts. Paracetamol does nothing on its own. I was on the combined pill which helped, but I got migraines with flashing zigzags, so the nurse stopped it two years ago.”

No previous surgery, no pelvic infections. Chlamydia test negative last year. Not pregnant (condoms; period 2 weeks ago). Non-smoker. Weight stable. No other medical problems. Migraines with aura about once every two months, none since stopping the pill… “maybe one”.
“My cousin had endometriosis. She needed IVF to have her little boy.”
“I manage a clothes shop. I’ve had an informal warning for sickness. I feel like they think I’m skiving.”
If asked: “I get low around periods — fed up, not depressed. No thoughts of harming myself.”

If asked what she thinks is going on or what worries her: “I’ve always been told it’s just bad periods, and I feel stupid for coming back. But I’ve read about endometriosis… my cousin had it. Will I be able to have children? We want to start trying in a year or two.”

Composed, a bit apologetic, expects to be brushed off. Do not raise the pain during sex unless asked sensitively. If the doctor says the scan was normal so it is probably nothing, become deflated and quiet. If the doctor explains that a normal scan does not rule out endometriosis, become visibly relieved (“So I’m not imagining it?”). Ask about fertility once you feel listened to. You are open to hormonal treatment if you understand it will not stop you having children later.

ice.ideas: Possibly endometriosis, like her cousin — but she has been told it is “just bad periods”.
ice.concerns: Fertility; losing her job; not being believed; the relationship.
ice.expectations: To be taken seriously and referred to someone who can find out what is going on.

cues: “I don’t really know what else can be done” — resignation after a normal scan.
“We’ve kind of stopped” — impact on the relationship.

checkpoints.text: Takes a focused history — timing and severity of pain, bleeding pattern, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms (dyschezia, rectal bleeding, haematuria), impact on daily life
Considers other causes and red flags (infection, fibroids, IBS, abnormal bleeding, pregnancy) and reviews the previous treatments and contraindications (migraine with aura)
Interprets the normal ultrasound correctly — it does not exclude endometriosis — and offers in-person abdominal and pelvic examination without delaying referral
Optimises analgesia — regular NSAID started before the pain with paracetamol, with safety advice
Offers hormonal treatment avoiding oestrogen (progestogen-only pill, LNG-IUS, implant or injection), explains it is reversible and compatible with future pregnancy plans
Refers to gynaecology (persistent symptoms affecting daily life, treatment limited, fertility concern), flagging cyclical bowel symptoms; safety-nets and arranges review
Validates her experience of being dismissed and acknowledges the impact on work, relationship and mood
Addresses the fertility worry honestly — many people with endometriosis conceive naturally, specialist input helps — and supports her with work (fit note, adjustments)

worked.txt: “Pain that stops you working is not ‘just bad periods’. I’m glad you came back.”
“Some people with painful periods also get pain during sex or opening their bowels. Is that something you’ve noticed?”
“A normal scan is useful — it rules out some things, like cysts — but it can’t rule out endometriosis, because small patches often don’t show on ultrasound.”
“Your symptoms fit endometriosis — where tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb and causes pain around periods.”

“Because of your migraines with aura, the combined pill isn’t safe for you, but progestogen-only options are — a daily pill, the hormonal coil, the implant or the injection. They don’t affect your fertility long-term.”
“Many people with endometriosis get pregnant without help. Seeing a gynaecologist now means you’ll have a plan well before you start trying.”

f.learning: Suspect endometriosis with chronic pelvic pain, period-related pain affecting daily life, deep dyspareunia, period-related painful bowel movements or painful urination, or infertility. A normal examination or ultrasound does not exclude it — refer anyway when symptoms are persistent, severe or affect daily life, or when initial treatment fails, is not tolerated or is contraindicated. Initial management runs in parallel with referral: NSAIDs and/or paracetamol, and hormonal treatment (combined hormonal contraception or a progestogen). In migraine with aura, combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 4, so use progestogen-only options. Suspected deep endometriosis involving bowel, bladder or ureter, or an endometrioma, should be referred to a specialist endometriosis service. Women often wait years for a diagnosis; listening and validating are part of the treatment. Discuss fertility honestly and consider work adjustments.

wordPics.fail: Recognises endometriosis as possible but repeats the scan or waits for further treatment trials before referral; or offers the combined pill despite migraine with aura.
wordPics.clearFail: Reassures that the normal scan means nothing is wrong; no referral; dismissive of her symptoms.

avoid.dont: “Your scan was normal, so that’s reassuring.”
avoid.instead: “The scan rules out some things, but it can’t rule out endometriosis.”
avoid.why: Normal imaging does not exclude endometriosis; false reassurance continues the delay.

avoid.dont: “Let’s restart the combined pill — it helped before.”
avoid.instead: “Because you get migraine with aura, oestrogen isn’t safe, but progestogen-only options are.”
avoid.why: Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 4 in migraine with aura (stroke risk).

avoid.instead: “Pain that stops you working isn’t something you should have to put up with.”
avoid.why: Normalising severe pain is the dismissal she has experienced for years.

model.text: Hello Sophie, I’m Dr Rahman. I can see you’ve been in about your periods before — tell me how things are now.
They’ve always been bad, but now I’m missing work every month. The scan was normal so I don’t know what else can be done.
Pain that stops you working isn’t something you should just put up with. Can you describe when the pain comes and how bad it gets?
Two days before I bleed, then four or five days. Eight or nine out of ten. I have to lie down.
Some people with painful periods also get pain deep inside during sex, or when opening their bowels or passing urine. Have you noticed any of those?
model.why: Sensitive enquiry into dyspareunia, dyschezia and dysuria

model.text: Yes — sex hurts deep down, we’ve kind of stopped. And it really hurts to open my bowels on my period.
Thank you for telling me. Any bleeding from the back passage or in your urine, bleeding between periods, or after sex? Any discharge or fevers?
And the treatments — I see the combined pill was stopped because of migraine with aura. How has the mefenamic acid been?
It takes the edge off. I take it when the pain starts.
What do you think might be going on?
I’ve read about endometriosis — my cousin had it and needed IVF. I’ve always been told it’s just bad periods.

I think you’re right to wonder about it. Your symptoms fit endometriosis — tissue similar to the womb lining growing outside the womb. The scan was useful, but endometriosis often doesn’t show on ultrasound, so a normal scan doesn’t rule it out.
model.why: Working diagnosis and correct interpretation of the normal scan

model.text: No, you’re not. Here’s what I suggest. First, pain relief: take naproxen regularly with food from the day before your period is due, plus paracetamol. Second, hormones can settle it — because of your migraines we’d avoid oestrogen, but a daily progestogen-only pill, the hormonal coil, the implant or the injection are all options. Third, I’ll refer you to gynaecology now, and mention the bowel symptoms.
model.why: Parallel analgesia, safe hormonal options and referral

model.text: Will the hormones stop me having a baby? We want to try in a year or two.

They don’t affect fertility long-term — you can stop them when you’re ready. Many people with endometriosis conceive naturally, and seeing the gynaecologist now means you’ll have a plan before you start trying.

I’d like to examine your tummy and pelvis in person, but that won’t hold up the referral. About work: I can provide a fit note suggesting adjustments, and Endometriosis UK has advice for employers. Let’s review in 6 weeks to see how the treatment is going, and contact us sooner if you get bleeding from the bowel or bladder, or severe pain that doesn’t settle.
model.why: Examination, work support, follow-up and safety-net

model.text: Thank you. That’s the first time I’ve felt listened to.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG73 Endometriosis: diagnosis and management (2017, updated 2024) · CoSRH UKMEC 2025 (migraine with aura and combined hormonal contraception) · ESHRE endometriosis guideline (2022)
knowledge.summary: Suspect endometriosis with period-related pain affecting daily life, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel or urinary symptoms, chronic pelvic pain or infertility. A normal examination or ultrasound does not exclude it. Start analgesia and hormonal treatment and refer in parallel.

points.t: Chronic pelvic pain; period-related pain affecting daily activities; deep pain during or after sex; period-related painful bowel movements or painful urination; period-related blood in urine or stool; infertility with any of these.

Offer abdominal and pelvic examination and transvaginal ultrasound (transabdominal if declined). Do not exclude endometriosis if both are normal. Do not use CA-125 or MRI to diagnose it in primary care.
A 3-month trial of an NSAID and/or paracetamol; start before the expected pain. Neuropathic agents and opioids are specialist decisions.

Combined hormonal contraception or a progestogen. In migraine with aura, combined methods are UKMEC 4 — use progestogen-only pill, LNG-IUS, implant or injection. Hormonal treatment does not harm future fertility.

If symptoms are severe, persistent or recurrent; pelvic signs; initial treatment ineffective, not tolerated or contraindicated; or fertility is a priority. Referral, imaging and treatment can happen in parallel.
Suspected or confirmed deep endometriosis involving bowel, bladder or ureter, endometrioma, or endometriosis outside the pelvis.
Many conceive naturally; specialist input helps plan. Surgery or assisted conception may be discussed depending on findings.
Ask about mood, relationships and work. Diagnosis often takes many years; validation matters.

social.t: Deep dyspareunia affects intimacy; offer to discuss with partner, and psychosexual support if wanted.

legal.t: Long-term conditions with substantial effect on daily activities may be a disability under the Equality Act 2010, which requires reasonable adjustments. A fit note can suggest adjustments.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice: listen to patients and take their views seriously. Repeated reassurance after normal tests contributes to delay.

community.t: Endometriosis UK (support groups, employer guidance); NHS endometriosis pages.

redFlags: Cyclical rectal bleeding or haematuria (deep disease)
Pelvic mass, weight loss, persistent bloating
ice: Concern: fertility; job; not being believed

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected endometriosis (severe dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia) despite normal transvaginal ultrasound; combined hormonal contraception contraindicated (migraine with aura).
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Endometriosis is where tissue like the lining of the womb grows in other places, like around the ovaries or bowel. It bleeds each month and causes pain. It often doesn’t show on scans.”

management.reflectIce: “You came expecting to be told it’s just bad periods again. I think it may be endometriosis, and I’m referring you.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note with adjustments; partner support; mood check.

Progestogen-only option of her choice (desogestrel, LNG-IUS, implant, injection)
Gynaecology referral now; in-person exam arranged
safetyNet: Rectal bleeding or haematuria with periods, severe unremitting pain → contact sooner

pitfalls.intro: The normal scan is the trap. Treating it as reassurance repeats years of dismissal.

items.fail: Interpreting the normal ultrasound as excluding endometriosis.
items.why: Ultrasound misses superficial disease; NICE says do not exclude on a normal scan.
items.fix: Explain what the scan can and cannot show; refer.

items.why: Migraine with aura makes combined methods UKMEC 4.

items.fail: Not asking about sex and bowel symptoms.
items.why: Deep dyspareunia and dyschezia support the diagnosis and may suggest deep disease.
These are her biggest worries and affect engagement.
items.fix: Ask what worries her most; respond honestly.

ro.d: Follows “I don’t really know what else can be done”, “we’ve kind of stopped” and “my cousin needed IVF”.
Idea (endometriosis, but told “just bad periods”); concern (fertility, job, not being believed, relationship); expectation (taken seriously and referred).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Fertility; losing her job; not being believed; the relationship — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
